Responses to reviewer # 1
Comments:

The topic of this manuscript is interesting; it’s about Neglected Diseases in children <5 years of age, which affect most underdeveloped countries, but mainly Africa. This paper is a cross-sectional study that describes determinants associated to undernutrition children <5 years of age that live in 14 villages located at the Eastern part of Cameroon whose main family activity is farming and fishing, one of the determinants described is STH and others are related to hygiene, income, access to clean water and other sociodemographic characteristics. If authors follow the comments below, will significantly improve the way their results are shown and may be easier for them and for the reader to understand them, discuss them and find conclusions.
Introduction

1. Authors point out this topic in the introduction section in page 2 lines 47-56. Although statistics about the STH infection preschool children are given, authors need to mention the prevalence of STH in Cameroon, because one of their outcomes (which isn’t the main one) is STH and it’s relevant to the sample size calculation. The opposite case is for undernutrition (page 2 lines 63 to 75), the main dependent variable described in this paper. Authors gave an explicit prevalence of its different stages children <5 years of age in the Eastern part of the country (58.3%), which makes the reader aware of the prevalence used for the sample size used and a result that would be expected in the study.

Reply: Yes, the prevalence of STH in Cameroon was indeed missing. The prevalence of STH (Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm, and Trichuris trichiura was 28.1%, 9.8%, and 6.3%, respectively in Cameroon. (Page 2, Lines 59-61). The prevalence used in calculation of the sample size was 50%. This prevalence will give a sample saize even bigger than the that of the 58.3% prevalence in the Eastern part of Cameroon. With this bigger sample size, our results tend to be more reliable.

2.It’s important to notice that authors use the term “malnutrition” to address undernutrition throughout the manuscript. WHO definition of malnutrition is: Malnutrition, in all its forms, includes undernutrition (wasting, stunting, underweight), inadequate vitamins or minerals, overweight, obesity, and resulting diet-related noncommunicable diseases. Thus, undernutrition is part of malnutrition but not equivalent. This study only explores undernutrition and its forms.

Reply: Thank you. We were mistakenly using the word malnutrition interchangeably with undernutrition. This comment has redirected us to focus on undernutrition which is the main goal in this manuscript. That has been corrected in the revised versión of the manuscript.

3.Authors only refer to overweight children under 5 years of age in page 2 line 72, which would also have been an interesting form to analyze in terms of income, inflammation, microbiota and life-style. But it’s understood that undernutrition forms were the most prevalent and a biological explanation for its correlation with STH is plausible.
Reply: Since overweight did not form part of our study, we took out that sentence so that readers are not distracted from our main goal which is undernutrition and its forms.
Material and methods

4. Authors describe that this manuscript shows the results of a part of a larger study whose main objective (mentioned in page 3 lines 86-87) wasn’t the one of this sub-analysis (mentioned in page 1 lines 73-75). Pointing out this aspect is important, mainly referring to limitations of the study, which aren’t mentioned by the authors in the discussion section.

Reply: Yes, this study was part of a larger study whose main objective is different from the analysis in the manuscript. A limitation of this study is that it was part of a larger study whose main objectives were not those of the sub-analysis which made it difficult to account for some unknown confounding variables. Secondly, due to the cross-sectional nature of the study, we could only discuss the association rather than causation. Thirdly, the present study was conducted only in one of the many health districts of Cameroon. Therefore, generalization of the results is difficult owing to the influence of regional characteristics on all aspects of the study. Fourthly, the faecal concentration technique employed for processing faecal samples do not yield data on parasite intensity but only on the prevalence rate. The methods were chosen for their efficiency and cost-effectiveness but are less sensitive than other commonly used procedures. Additional technique such as Kato-Katz would have been able to provide useful data on the relative intensity of infections. Lastly, another important limitation of our study is that the generalizability of our finding is limited to young children (12–59 months), which might result in different risk factors in other age groups. These lmitations are indicated as track corrections in the discusion section of the text (Page 18, Lines 420-427)

5. Also, apart from the informed consent from mothers and the voluntary participation of subjects, other selection criteria (inclusion, exclusion and elimination) weren’t mentioned (eg. incomplete data, outliers, known acquired immunodeficiencies, genetic diseases, mental diseases, withdrawal of consent, etc., variables that are important to take into account for the selection of the o that need to be measured because they may be confounders).

Reply: With respect to inclusion, exclusion and elimination criteria, children aged 12-59 months whose parents gave their consent and who had lived in the area for more than 6 months were selected for the study. Children who presented with a detectable handicap that could alter linear growth were excluded from the study. If parents of selected children withdrew informed consent forms or were absent during the household visit, those children were replaced. Children who were not resident of the study area, but were visiting, and children of families who had moved into the study area within the past 3 month were also eliminated from the study population. These criteria are indicated in the study design section of the revised manuscript (Page 3, Lines 87-99).

6. In page 3 lines 88 to 92 is mentioned that anthropometric, demographic socioeconomic and parasitological data were collected from mothers of the children. It is understood that parasitological data come from each child’s stool sample, not from their mother. On the other hand, it is mentioned that the rest of the information was obtained from structured questionnaires and clinical evaluation. Were mothers interviewed or was the questionnaire of self-response? It’s important to point out what happened with mothers with no formal education; were they able to read the questionnaire or were they interviewed?.

Reply: Thank you for your comment. Subjects in each household were registered and anthropometric, demographic and parasitological data of each child were collected while socio-economic data came from the mothers of the children as principal respondents following administration of questionnaires. This precision has been made in the text (Page 3, Lines 96-99)). Interpreters (who were selected community relay agents, familiar to the people), were used to translate and interpret the questions on the questionnaires to the kakor dialect for mothers who had no formal education and could not understand neither French nor pidgin English (Please see Page 3, Line 99-102).

7. Authors mention that the socio-demograhic questionnaire was corrected/modified after a pilot study/analysis (page 3 lines 105-108). In this sense, for questions addressing hand washing habit and shoe wearing habits, did the “sometimes” response have an indication, like 2 or three times a day or a week? This may be clarified as note at the end of the corresponding table. For hand washing habit is clear that this variable could be correlated to meal frequency but correlation analysis should be done to discard it and to make a correct model of adjusted logistic regression (which authors mention that was done but the variables used in the adjusted model weren’t mentioned throughout the manuscript) if that’s the case.

Reply: Yes, we fully agree that hand washing habit and meal frequency could be correlated. However, in the revision of the manuscript, we used multinomial logistic regression to assess the risk factors for undernutrition and logistic regression for the helminth infections. In both models, these variables were not in the final model as could see in the results section.

8. Authors describe how they calculated the sample size (page 3 lines 93 to 97) and they used a prevalence of 50% of “malnutrition” (which is inferred as undernutrition). It is not clear the source of the prevalence (eg. a previous study) or if it is the prevalence used because its value is unknown. Nonetheless, authors mention in the introduction section that the overall prevalence of undernutrition was slightly higher (58.3%) than 50%. When calculating sample size, a description of the source of the parameter used (%, variance, RR, etc.) should be given or referred. Sample size is calculated according to a parameter of the dependent variable, which is undernutrition mainly throughout the manuscript, but STH is also used as a dependent variable from which no prevalence value was given in the introduction section and should be considered for the sample size calculation if correlation and association analyses are planned. Authors mention the sample size with 10% of non-responses was of 422 children.

Reply: The prevalence of STH in general is not known but the prevalence of Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm, and Trichuris trichiura is 28.1%, 9.8%, and 6.3%, respectively in Cameroon [4]. ((Page 2, Lines 59-61)The sample size description, we considered the prevalence of 50% to have the maximum sample as we know that considering the 58.3%, the corresponding sample size will be less than the current 422 included in our study. In addition, the prevalence of soil-transmitted helminths in Cameroon is greater than the prevalence of undernutrition. Therefore, its corresponding sample size will be also less than 422. In conclusion, we think the current sample size is enough to answer research questions regarding the nutritional status and the helminths infections.

9. Authors describe the anthropometrics assessment (page 4 lines 117 to 135) but a clarification in this section regarding WHZ, WAZ and HAZ and the parameter they reflect (stunting, underweight or wasting) is needed. Also that the abbreviation “SAM” stands for Severe Acute Malnutrition.

Reply: Thank you for your comment. The different parameters WHZ, WAZ, HAZ correspond respectively to Weight-for-Height, Weight- for-Age, and Height-for-Age according to WHO 2006 standards [13]. They reflect respectively wasting, underweight and stunting respectively. They haven been explained in the text. (Page 4 Lines 143-144) ) . Write SAM abbreviated as Severe acute malnutrition has been indicated in the text (Page 4 Lines 144-150) .

10. Throughout the manuscript is mentioned that 422 children were analyzed but in the section that describes the anthropometrics assessment, is mentioned that outliers for WHZ, WAZ and HAZ were excluded. This is confusing because readers expect to find less than 422 participants because of the exclusion of outliers, and the n was mentioned as constant for all results.

Reply: Thanks for your comment. We have checked and indeed, they were 2 outliers for WHZ and WAZ, respectively, while no outlier was found for HAZ when applying the rule as an outlier has z-score less than – 6 or greater than 6. Therefore, we used the total sample size (422) for Table 1 (Page 8, Line 230), descriptive statistics, and risk factor for helminth infections. However, these outliers were excluded when assessing the determinant for undernutrition, stunting, wasting and underweight.
11. In the direct microscopy section (page 4 line 142), the “normal saline” must include in brackets (0.85% Sodium Chloride) as it is referred for the formal saline (page 5 line 15).
Reply: ‘0.85% of Sodium Chloride’ has been put in brackets in the manuscript (Page 5 Line 158) as suggested by the reviewer.

12. Authors describe the statistical analyses in page 5 lines 165-167. Cross-sectional studies mainly describe the distribution of variables in the study population and between groups. Thus, first there is a description of which central trend parameters are going to be calculated (mean, standard deviation, median, min-max quartiles, skweness, etc), units of meausrement, considerations to group continuous variables (eg. age) in certain intervals, comparison tests (between means or proportions), association tests to be made, which is the dependent variable, its characteristics (continuous, categories), and which is/are the main independent variable(s) or covariables. Also the level of significance is mentioned. Authors described part of the analyses (which was extensive and shown in 14 tables) made but omitted to describe how they handled variables like age (mother and child) and why they were grouped the way are shown in tables for example. Also, authors mention two dependent variables (first STH and then “malnutrition”), from which only one out of 14 tables depicts the analysis for STH. Authors mention that a logistic regression analysis (binary and adjusted) was done. It is important to note that none of the tables that show logistic regression results specifies the covariables used to adjust (the final model) and this is a n important point because of correlations between them and main effects in the model. Authors mention that is a multivariate logistic regression. The way results are depicted, seems that authors meant multiple or multivariable logistic regression model, which finds the equation that best predicts the success value of the binary response or one outcome variable (dependent) for the values of several independent variables (covariables). As it is understood from the manuscript’s tables, the dependent variable undernutrition has a binary outcome (yes/no), and also their forms (stunting, undernutrition and wasting). On the other hand, multivariate analysis is used for the analysis with more than one outcome (eg, repeated measures) and multiple independent variables. According to the study design, repeated measures were not done. These terms are usually mentioned as equivalent but are mathematically different. Authors omitted the level of significance. In this section and in the discussion section independent variables are considered risk factors, but prevalence odds ratio don’t reflect probability (causality). Also, authors should consider that Fisher’s exact test is also used to compare proportions but when there are <5 observations per category, a situation that is shown in table 6.

Reply: Thanks for your comment. We have updated the manuscript statistical methodology (Page 5 Lines 180-206) under statistical analyses section according to reviewer’s comments. To this end, we emphasized the descriptive statistics used (proportions) and how the continuous variables were recoded into categorical. Also, we highlighted the different outcomes and potential predictors to be used in assessing the relationship between the main outcomes and these determinants. As you mentioned, univariate and multiple logistic regression were performed, and the strategy was to include in the multiple logistic regression, those variables with a p-value less than 25% in the univariate analysis. In addition, we considered a multinomial logistic regression to assess the risk factor of undernutrition when using the different forms of nutritional status as one categorical vriables and composed of normal (reference), stunting, wasting and underweight. The level of significance used was 5%.
Results

13. Results of the 422 participants are interesting and observations show the lack of progress in preventing STH and undernutrition. Even though authors use adjectives like many, most and majority in the description of results, the lack of % (n/N) values makes it hard to follow the narrative with the corresponding table and may lead to the description of non-frequent categories that may be used to draw conclusions, like the water source: the use of public tap (58.3%, 246/422) was more frequent than the spring or well (41.5%; 176/422) (page 5 line 183). It is possible to rearrange the narrative to point out the most frequent characteristics of the population, like the fact that most of them (93.1%; 393/422) are farmers, an observation that may be used to explain some of the results obtained in the logistic regression.

Reply: Thank you for this comment. The narrative has been rearranged to point out the most frequent characteristic parameter in the population as recommended by the reviewer (See descriptive statistics Page 6, Lines 209-228). For this, The n/N value has been included accordingly into each of the tables to clearly describe the frequent categories and these frequencies have been arranged to show the most frequent characteristics. Frequencies have been given in percentages and ratios (Page 6, Lines 209-229 and has been used to explain some results of the logistic regression. The significance of the fact that most parents are farmers has been discussed at the level of discussion.

14. There are too many tables and some may be combined, eg. Tables 1, 2 and 3, because the three of them describe the population. The column “Frequency” should include the total n (n=422) because all n values in each category are distributed around 422 participants. Maternal parity total n is different from 422 (it’s 367) and total % is 87%. Some data is missing for this variable. In this regard, authors should check that the % of all variables sums up 100%, there are some variables with 100.1 % to100.6%.

Thanks for your comment. We have merged Tables 1,2 and 3, as the three indeed describe the population. In addition, we have checked carefully and corrected the proportion of all variable sums (see Table 1 in the revised manuscript Page 7).

15. Regarding information included in table 2, is important to note that there are no anthropometric data shown in it (as it is specified in the title), anthropometric data are shown in figures 1 and 2 (that also can be merged).

Reply: Thanks for your comment. We fully agree that information included in Table 2 (Previous) socio-demographic data instead of anthropometric data. Therefore, we merged Table 2 with Tables 1 and 3 and to give Table 1 (Revised manuscript) the title updated to describe the socio-demographic characteristics that describe the participants (Page 7).

16. All tables that show results of logistic regression (for undernutrition and its forms) need the n in the “Category” column (n=422) and the n in each row that corresponds to each category of each variable. Also, another column is needed, the frequency (%) of each category. Also a p value for chi square can be integrated if columns are added. These additions are important because authors mention frequencies in the descriptive narrative and compare them between groups and conclude differences, like the narrative in page 9 lines 228-232. In this regard, Table 4, the one described in this paragraph, doesn’t show analysis according to gender and in the paragraph these results are mentioned (should be “data not in tables”).

Reply: Thanks for your comment. Table 2 now (revised manuscript Page 9)) describes the health/nutritional status of the children who participated in the study. We have updated all the tables resulting from the logistic regression accordingly (Table 2 of the revised manuscript) and included the n values corresponding to each category of undernutrition and its form. As recommended, another column is added corresponding to the frequency (%) of each category). However, considering that there is only one variable here, we did not go to do Chi squared teast but has used descriptive statistics.

17. The column of the dependent variables (undernutrition, stunting and waisting, intestinal parasitic infection) needs the n value of each one. Also, all tables must include footnotes that describe the abbreviations (UOR, AOR) and should mention the variables used in the final model (adjusted model) because the lack of this information makes the adjustment unclear and conclusions of the results of logistic regression analysis not strong. Also, should be careful with the OR interpretation, for eg. page 9 line 231, mentions that younger children are most affected by undernutrition; the unadjusted OR is higher than 1 for older children, but when adjusted is lower than one. Without the n value of each category, the % and the variables used in the adjusted model, this interpretation isn’t clear. In Table 4, the upper limit of the third interval of age should be 59 months and shows information named anthropometric and I’m not sure if it is that type of information in an attempt to link it with the methods section that describe the “anthropometrics assessment”.

Reply: n values have been added to all tables with dependent variables (Tables 3 and 4 of revised version Pages 11 and 12 respectively). To tables 3,5 and 6 (revised version Pages 11, 12 and 15), foot notes have been included to describe abbreviations: UOR=Unadjusted Odds Ratio, AOR=Adjusted Odds Ratio, CI=Confidence Interval.. Table 4 (in the revised version) shows the univariate analysis of the different soil-transmitted helminth infections based on child gender.

In the entire text, the upper limit for the third interval of age has been corrected to be 59 months and not 60. For clarity, the variable of age has been removed from anthropometric data to demographic data.

18. I consider that Tables a, b, c and d can be merged in a wide table in a first attempt to organize data, because all share the same independent variables. This may be an easier way to compare results between undernutrition and its forms and write the narrative of the results as brief and right (with %, n/N and ORs CI05%) as possible to be able to discuss results and conclude. On the other hand, the narrative that describes the results of the four tables needs to be revised (page 10 lines 245 to 248), eg, for adjusted ORs, low income has no significant association with underweight, seven or more household members is not associated to stunting or wasting, less than three meals per day is not associated to wasting. If n and % values are shown for each category and analyzed, maybe authors can find if n values give no associations or there’s a need to look for an explanation in the discussion section. It’s possible that the only table that brings a group result and a solid conclusion is the one for undernutrition and there is no need to include the forms of it (the rest of the tables or make a wide one). Authors must thoroughly analyze these results to include those important for the manuscript.

Reply: Tables 5a, b, c and d have been merged into a wide single table (Table 3 Page 11) in the revised manuscript) in order to facillitatate comparison of results between undernutrition and its forms. The narrative describing the table has been revised after performing multinomial logistic regression with nutritional status as outcome and sociodemographic factors as predictors.

19. To follow a sequence of results that can lead to a better understanding of the prevalence of the infection, the order of the rows may be modified in Table 6, eg., first show the overall infection, second the single infection, and so on. Table 6 shows an analysis according to gender, which isn’t described in the narrative of the table but gender differences are discussed in the discussion section as an important variable but for undernutrition mainly because of the results of table 8a. Chi square values aren’t usually included in tables and in the narrative should be stated that there are no differences between the infection characteristics.

Reply: For a better comprehension, the updated table 6 (now Table 4 in the revised version Page 12) shows the overall infection before the single and multiple infection. Chi square values have been taken off the table and analysis of the table according to gender did not reveal gender-related differences with respect to infection (Page 12, Lines 273).

20. Bold font should be in fingernail cleanliness results in Table 7 and normal font in water contact results. Authors omitted the significant result for spring water source a topic discussed in the discussion section. Underweight was the form of undernutrition with significant association with infection and undernutrition variable was not included in the table, while in the narrative is described.

Reply: Bold font size has been given to fingernail cleanliness results (see Table 5 revised version) and normal font for water contact. In a repeat of the statistical analys by a more experienced statistician, only the fingernails variable was found to influence undernutrition. The effect of spring water source was found not to significantly influence undernutrition (Table 5). We prefer to address the issue of underweight as a form of undernutrition with significant association with infection and undernutrition variable in Table 6.

21. Tables 8a, b, c and d can be merged in a wide table as they share independent variables in a first attempt to organize, describe data, discuss and conclude. The narrative that describes the results of these tables mentions they’re from binary logistic regression but numbers shown are of the adjusted model. Authors also mention that children with intestinal parasites are 2.92 times “at risk” to present undernutrition (page 17 line 322). Risk implies probability, thus causality and prevalence odds ratio don’t. These children have 2.92 higher odds of undernutrition. The narrative describes the associations for undernutrition but not for its forms, which show different significant associations than the ones described in the narrative.

Reply: Thanks for your comment. We have merged Tables 8a, b, and c into one table (Table 6 in the revised version) as they share independent variables. The narrative previously described as a binary logistic regression has been modified to describe the result of a multinomial logistic regression performed with nutritional status as outcome. following a more guided statistical analysis by a more experienced statistitian, the above results were not verified. The following results (Table 6, Page 15), the presence of ascaris infection did not significantly impact the nutritional status of the child at the 5% significance level. Nonetheless, the gender of the child and the type of toilet had a significant impact on stunting (OR=0.49; CI=0.25-0.94) and wasting (OR=0.40; CI=0.20-0.77) respectively.
Discussion

22. Page 21 line 393 needs a capital letter and page 22 lines 418 to 420 discusses a result that was not studied, described or analyzed. It’s not clear why authors included this paragraph in the discussion section. The discussion around undernutrition in the study population is centered in lack of knowledge and education on balanced diets, but results suggest that low income that is related to low frequency of daily meals, access to education higher than elementary and lack of clean water sources may be the main association with infection. It could have been interesting to know the variables included in the adjusted model, their correlation and explanation.

Reply: Considering that a more experienced statistician carried out the statistical analyses, the results presented in this revised version are different from the ones initially submitted. Thus, the comment on capital letter for Page 21, Line 393 as well as the discussion of an undescribed data on 22 lines 418 to 420 do not longer apply. A full-fledged discussion based on the results of the present statistics is presented and no longer based on undernutrition in the study population being centered in lack of knowledge and education on balanced diets.

We re-analyzed the data grouping tables 1, 2 and 3 to describe the characteristics of the study participants. With these changes, Table 2 now describes the health/nutritional status of the children who participated in the study. Table 3 describes the presents results after performing multinomial logistic regression with nutritional status as outcome and socio-demographic factors as predictors. Tables 4 has been updated to describe the univariate analysis of the different soil-transmitted helminth infections based on child gender. Table 5 has been modified to show the risk factors of intestinal parasitic infections in children while table 6, shows the association of intestinal parasites and nutritional status. All these modifications have been discussed at the level of the Discussion in the manuscript.
